one_liner: Open-source C++/Python quantum chemistry suite; in one 2020 community benchmark its non-DF B3LYP run edged out GAMESS-US.
what_it_does: Psi4 computes ab initio molecular energies, gradients and properties (Hartree-Fock, DFT, MP2, coupled cluster, SAPT and more) from a Python driver over a C++ core exported through pybind11. You run it as a program (psi4 job.in, the 'Psithon' input) or import it as a Python module (PsiAPI) and call psi4.energy('b3lyp/6-31g*'). It is a different program from GAMESS-US with its own input language and defaults, so 'switching' means rewriting inputs, not linking a library.
how_it_is_fast: SCF and DFT cost is dominated by building the Coulomb and exchange (J/K) matrices and the exchange-correlation quadrature. Psi4 offers several JK algorithms, from conventional PK (pre-sorted integral supermatrix), DIRECT and OUT_OF_CORE to density fitting (DF, its default for SCF and DFT) and newer composite builders (DFDIRJ+COSX, DFDIRJ+LINK, sn-LinK through GauXC); integrals come from Libint2, DFT grids from gau2grid with Libxc functionals, and the heavy lifting is OpenMP-threaded BLAS/LAPACK (MKL in the conda binaries). In the benchmark the advantage over GAMESS-US came mainly from thread scaling: Psi4 ran 12.1x faster on 16 cores than on 1, GAMESS-US 8.5x (derived from page data).
when_to_use: Medium-sized molecules (tens of atoms, up to a few thousand basis functions per the README) on one multi-core node, where Psi4's OpenMP scaling beat GAMESS-US's socket build by 1.27x at 8 cores and 1.50x at 16 in the C20 B3LYP test.
When you need a free, LGPL-3.0 code that you can script from Python (PsiAPI, NumPy interop) for high-throughput or method-development workflows instead of a commercial package.
Intermolecular interaction work (SAPT family) and density-fitted SCF/MP2, which are Psi4's default and best-tuned paths.
Installs via conda on Linux (x86-64 and ARM64), macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), Windows and WSL.
when_not_to_use: If raw single-node SCF/DFT speed is the goal: in the same table Psi4 1.3 was slower than ORCA 4, Turbomole 7, Q-Chem 5 and Gaussian 09 at every core count (726.2 vs 195.6 for Q-Chem at 1 core, 60.2 vs 14.2 for Turbomole at 16), and slower than Gaussian 16 at 1 to 4 cores.
On 1 to 4 cores against GAMESS-US the difference is about 5% (1.05x), within what different convergence criteria or BLAS builds could explain.

Multi-node runs: the top-level CMakeLists.txt exposes ENABLE_OPENMP and no MPI option, so one calculation runs on one machine; in the benchmark, ORCA, NWChem, Firefly and Dalton were the OpenMPI builds.

If you want the benchmarked configuration: it measured Psi4 with density fitting turned off, which is not how Psi4 runs by default, so the numbers do not describe ordinary Psi4 usage in either direction.

integration.form: module (Python package with a compiled C++ core library); conda binaries or a CMake build
integration.dependencies: BLAS/LAPACK (MKL in conda builds), Python with NumPy, pybind11, Libint2 (with Eigen and Boost headers), Libxc, gau2grid, QCElemental and qcengine, plus runtime networkx, pint, pydantic, msgpack, SciPy, py-cpuinfo and psutil; many optional add-ons
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 compiler and CMake 3.19+ on current master; Python 3.10 to 3.14 per the README
integration.platforms: Linux (x86-64, ARM64), macOS (Intel, Apple Silicon), Windows and WSL per the README
integration.thread_safety: Parallel inside one calculation via OpenMP (thread count set by the user); the Python driver keeps global option state (core.set_global_option), so run concurrent calculations as separate processes; not otherwise documented in the files read

gotchas: Harness flaw: the benchmark turned density fitting off for Psi4, yet Psi4's driver switches SCF_TYPE to DF whenever the user has not set it (proc_util.py in v1.3.2 and on master), and the README does not say which conventional algorithm (PK, DIRECT or OUT_OF_CORE) replaced it; there are no input files to check.

Not an equal-accuracy comparison: Psi4 1.3.2's energy() converges SCF to 1e-6 in energy and 1e-6 in the orbital-gradient density criterion on a 75 x 302 unpruned grid, GAMESS-US converges on the SCF density change, and Gaussian 16 uses UltraFine grids and 1e-12 integral accuracy (README note); each package used its own defaults.

Different builds and math libraries: Psi4 is listed only as 'Build-in Multithreading in Python 3.7', most likely the conda binary, which per the v1.3.2 conda docs ships with MKL and statically linked BLAS, while GAMESS-US was compiled with GNU 4.8.5, OpenBLAS 0.3.10 and socket parallelism; single runs, no units, and an implausible Dalton row (1502.0 s at 1 core, 6215.0 at 2) further weaken the harness.

Stale versions: the table is Psi4 1.3 from an October 2020 run; Psi4 is at v1.11 (2026-06-29) and has since added DFDIRJ+COSX, DFDIRJ+LINK and GauXC sn-LinK exchange builders and faster range-separated DirectJK, none of which were measured.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling in sparse-and-solvers is a quantum chemistry code (they are sparse BLAS, direct solvers and QP solvers), and Psi4's hot paths are dense BLAS and integral kernels, so this entry sits in the category only loosely; pick Psi4 when you need a whole electronic-structure program, not a solver library.
verified_claims_summary: In the r2compchem/benchmark-qm table (October 2020, AMD Threadripper 1950X, 16 cores, SMT on, 32 GB), a single-point B3LYP/6-31G(d) energy of C20 with density fitting off took Psi4 1.3 726.2, 193.2 and 60.2 (units not stated, presumably seconds) at 1, 4 and 16 cores vs 766.2, 202.0 and 90.1 for GAMESS-US 2020 (GNU 4.8.5, OpenBLAS 0.3.10), so 1.05x at 1-4 cores and 1.50x at 16 (derived from page data). Each package ran with its own convergence and grid defaults and the Psi4 build is not described.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-08, v1.11 released 2026-06-29, about 16k commits, 384 open issues) and LGPL-3.0, easy to install from conda; the speed evidence is a small, input-less 2020 community benchmark of a non-default, now-stale configuration, which fits tier B only as an independent measurement and gives a 5 to 50 percent edge over a baseline outside the category.
